claims.text: Conventional analytical conductivity models for bulk HfNbTaTiZr are based on perfect, defect-free crystal structures.
Explicitly incorporating defect scattering and oxygen impurity effects will improve conductivity-prediction accuracy for HfNbTaTiZr relative to conventional analytical models.
The expected accuracy improvement applies in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Defect scattering is expected to dominate electron transport in HfNbTaTiZr at 0–200 K.
At 300–1200 K, both intrinsic lattice vibrations and thermally activated defect dynamics contribute to transport.
Oxygen impurities and other defects locally distort the HfNbTaTiZr lattice.
Defect-induced local lattice distortions increase electron scattering.
At low temperatures, enhanced scattering from oxygen and other defects lowers electrical conductivity.
At high temperatures, thermally activated defect dynamics further modify electrical transport.
Representing oxygen and defect-induced distortions will adjust predicted conductivity closer to experimental measurements.
The defect-inclusive model will predict lower conductivity than the ideal defect-free model.
A specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen will have measurably lower conductivity than a nominally pristine HfNbTaTiZr specimen.
The defect-inclusive model will reduce prediction discrepancy across both stated temperature regimes.
The approach is applicable from approximately 0 to 1200 K.
The approach is applicable to nearly ideal specimens and specimens containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Predictions may be unreliable above 1200 K or at oxygen concentrations above approximately 1 wt.%.
Limited detailed experimental characterization leaves the actual defect structures and possible secondary-phase contributions uncertain.
